## Comparación gráfica: Normal vs $t$ de Student

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center
x <- seq(-5, 5, length = 500)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1), family = "sans")
plot(x, dnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#1b4d2e",
     ylim = c(0, 0.42),
     xlab = "t / z", ylab = "Densidad",
     main = "Normal estándar vs t de Student con distintos grados de libertad",
     cex.main = 1.15, cex.lab = 1.1)
cols <- c("#dc2626","#b45309","#1e3a8a","#6d28d9")
dfs  <- c(3, 5, 15, 30)
for (i in seq_along(dfs))
  lines(x, dt(x, dfs[i]), lwd = 2, col = cols[i], lty = i+1)
abline(v = c(-1.96, 1.96), col = "#1b4d2e", lwd = 1.5, lty = 3)
legend("topright",
       legend = c("Normal(0,1)", paste0("t(df=", dfs, ")")),
       col = c("#1b4d2e", cols), lwd = c(3,2,2,2,2),
       lty = c(1,2,3,4,5), bty = "n", cex = 1.05)
box(col = "gray40")
```

<div class="block-note fragment fade-up mt-8" data-fragment-index="1">
<div class="block-body text-center" style="font-size: 25px;">
La $t$ tiene <strong>colas más pesadas</strong> que la Normal: da valores críticos mayores y produce ICs más anchos. Con $df \geq 30$ las diferencias son menores al 5%; para $df \geq 100$ son despreciables.
</div>
</div>
